title: France and the 1994 Rwandan Genocide
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The role of France in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda has caused much trouble and debate. Before the mass killings, France gave help and weapons to the government of President Juvénal Habyarimana.
pages.caption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

imageProvenance.credit: DoD photo by: SSGT ANDY DUNAWAY

evidence.articleCaption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

pages.text: French leaders worried about the Rwandan Patriotic Front, a rebel group led mostly by Tutsi exiles. France gave training and arms to the government soldiers and other groups during the civil war.

When the genocide began in April 1994, France started an operation to move foreigners out of the country. During this mission, French troops left Tutsi spouses behind at checkpoints where they were killed.

Later in June 1994, France started a United Nations mission called Operation Turquoise to make a safe zone for people in danger. While this zone saved many lives, critics said it also helped killers escape.
After these events, relations between France and Rwanda stayed very tense for a long time. Rwanda later closed French schools and changed its main school language from French to English.

Years later, official panels in France studied these events. A report in 2021 found that France was not complicit in the genocide, though it bore responsibility for not breaking with the regime sooner.

The involvement of France in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda has remained a subject of ongoing controversy and diplomatic tension. Prior to the mass killings, Paris maintained close military and political ties with the Hutu-led government of President Juvénal Habyarimana, viewing the advancing Rwandan Patriotic Front as a destabilizing force.
pages.caption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

imageProvenance.credit: DoD photo by: SSGT ANDY DUNAWAY

evidence.articleCaption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

pages.text: During the civil war, France provided weapons and training to government forces and allied militias. Investigators later noted that many official arms deliveries during this period were approved without following standard regulatory rules.

When the genocide erupted following the April 1994 plane crash, France launched a military operation to evacuate foreign nationals. However, critics condemned the operation because foreign forces refused to rescue Tutsi spouses and left them at checkpoints to be killed.

Near the end of the hundred-day genocide in June 1994, France launched Operation Turquoise, a UN-mandated intervention establishing a humanitarian zone in southwestern Rwanda. While the mission saved thousands of lives, critics argued it also allowed genocide perpetrators to escape into neighboring Zaire.

Tensions severely damaged diplomatic relations between the two countries for years. The Rwandan government subsequently closed French cultural institutions, shifted the primary school language to English, and joined the Commonwealth.

Subsequent investigations, including a 2021 report commissioned by French President Emmanuel Macron, concluded that while France bore responsibility for failing to break with the regime sooner, there was no evidence of French complicity in the genocide itself.

C1-C2.headline: Diplomatic and Military Fallout: France in Rwanda

pages.text: The intricate and contentious relationship between France and Rwanda surrounding the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi has generated sustained diplomatic friction. Historical records indicate that French officials perceived the RPF insurgency from Uganda as an Anglophone threat to a Francophone ally, prompting substantial military and political backing for President Juvénal Habyarimana's government.
pages.caption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

imageProvenance.credit: DoD photo by: SSGT ANDY DUNAWAY

evidence.articleCaption: A French marine, part of the international force supporting the relief effort for Rwandan refugees, adjusts the concertina wire surrounding the airport.

pages.text: Investigative findings and parliamentary records show that many weapons deliveries to Kigali bypassed standard regulatory controls. Furthermore, French personnel provided training to elite units meant to counter the RPF, though subsequent reports emphasized that these officers had no direct involvement in the atrocities.

In the immediate wake of the assassinations on April 6, 1994, France initiated Operation Amaryllis to evacuate expatriates. The mission drew severe criticism for abandoning local Tutsi spouses at government checkpoints and destroying sensitive embassy documents prior to evacuation.

As the genocide neared its conclusion, France deployed Operation Turquoise under a United Nations mandate to establish a secure humanitarian zone. While the intervention successfully sheltered thousands of refugees, analysts emphasize that it simultaneously impeded RPF military momentum and facilitated the escape of genocidal perpetrators into Zaire.

The long-term fallout witnessed a profound diplomatic rupture, characterized by the closure of French institutions in Rwanda, a linguistic transition from French to English in the national education system, and Rwanda's accession to the Commonwealth.

In March 2021, the commission finished its report, concluding that France bore responsibility for failing to break with the regime sooner. However, the report found no evidence of French complicity in the genocide itself, as investigators examined state archives to assess institutional accountability during that turbulent period.

pages.text: Cultural heritage institutions and individuals take care of cultural property. Proper storage helps objects live longer with less damage and degradation. Keepers of these items know best practices to preserve them in their original state.
pages.caption: Liebieghaus Depot collection storage

evidence.articleCaption: Liebieghaus Depot collection storage

pages.text: Creating a storage space involves looking at available resources and collection needs. Good storage is separate from other activities to stop potential damage from theft, tracked in soil, and excessive light exposure.
pages.caption: Items being stored on shelves and the floor at the Australian War Memorial's Treloar Resource Centre

evidence.fileTitle: File:Shelves of military equipment at the Treloar Technology Centre in September 2012.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: Items being stored on shelves and the floor at the Australian War Memorial's Treloar Resource Centre

pages.text: Climate control systems help keep temperature and relative humidity at a steady rate. This stops materials from expanding and shrinking, which can cause serious damage to the objects.
pages.caption: Hygrothermograph

evidence.articleCaption: Hygrothermograph

pages.text: Storage spaces tend to have few windows and lights to protect items. LED or UV-filtered fluorescent bulbs are recommended because they save energy and protect objects from heat and radiation.

evidence.articleCaption: MN Warsaw. Interior painting store. 1966

pages.text: Institutions use integrated pest management to monitor for insects and rodents that may harm collections. They use traps to check for pests and eliminate entrances, using chemical treatments only as a last resort.

Cultural heritage institutions and individuals are responsible for storing cultural property properly. Good storage ensures a longer lifespan for objects with minimal damage, relying on the keepers' knowledge of preservation practices.

pages.text: Because light damage is cumulative and irreversible, storage areas limit ambient light and use multi-zone switches. LED and UV-filtered fluorescent bulbs are recommended to save energy and avoid harmful heat.

Integrated pest management programs monitor for insects and rodents using traps. Chemical treatments are kept as a last resort, and institutions avoid exterior lighting that might attract pests to doors and windows.

The preservation of cultural property falls primarily to heritage institutions and individuals. Proper storage mitigates degradation and extends object lifespans, guided by keepers' expertise in best practices for diverse artifacts and materials.

title: Facts About Mercury
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Mercury is a special chemical element with the symbol Hg and atomic number 80. It is also known as quicksilver. It is a heavy and silvery metal. Most metals are solid, but mercury is the only metallic element known to be liquid at standard temperature and pressure conditions.
pages.caption: Color lines in a spectral range

evidence.articleCaption: Color lines in a spectral range

pages.text: Mercury occurs in natural deposits around the world. It is mostly found as a mineral called cinnabar. People can grind cinnabar to make a bright red pigment. Exposure to mercury and its compounds is toxic. It can harm the nervous system, immune system, and kidneys of humans and animals.
pages.caption: A round pound coin (density ~7.6 g/cm) floats on mercury due to the buoyancy force upon it and appears to float higher because of the strong surface tension of the mercury.

evidence.articleCaption: A round pound coin (density ~7.6 g/cm) floats on mercury due to the buoyancy force upon it and appears to float higher because of the strong surface tension of the mercury.

pages.text: For a long time, mercury was used in many everyday devices. People put it in thermometers, barometers, and old light bulbs. Because it is toxic, manufacturers now use much less mercury or avoid it completely. However, it is still used in some scientific research and dental fillings.
pages.caption: Native mercury with cinnabar, Socrates mine, Sonoma County, California. Cinnabar sometimes alters to native mercury in the oxidized zone of mercury deposits.

evidence.articleCaption: Native mercury with cinnabar, Socrates mine, Sonoma County, California. Cinnabar sometimes alters to native mercury in the oxidized zone of mercury deposits.

pages.text: Mercury has very low melting and boiling points compared to other metals. Solid mercury can be cut with a knife because it is soft and malleable. It does not conduct heat very well, but it is a fair conductor of electricity. Iron containers are traditionally used to transport it.
pages.caption: Evolution of mercury price (U.S.) and production (worldwide)

evidence.articleCaption: Evolution of mercury price (U.S.) and production (worldwide)

pages.text: People have known about mercury for a very long time. Ancient people found it in Egyptian tombs dating back to 1500 BC. Cinnabar has been used by humans since the Neolithic Age. Today, scientists understand its risks better, so its use in medicine and daily life has greatly decreased.

Due to growing toxicity concerns, manufacturers have significantly reduced its usage or eliminated it entirely. Although historical medicines frequently incorporated mercury compounds, understanding of its toxicity has led to a major decline in its medical and industrial applications today.

Direct exposure or biomagnification of water-soluble forms results in severe toxicity affecting the nervous and immune systems, as well as human and animal renal functions.

pages.text: Although traditionally incorporated into various measuring instruments, electrical switches, and lighting systems, mounting toxicity concerns have prompted manufacturers to curtail or eliminate mercury usage. Despite these reductions, it continues to serve specific functions in scientific research and certain dental restorations.

A1-A2.headline: What is drug policy around the world

pages.text: A drug policy is the way governments and other groups control and regulate drugs. These are substances that can cause addiction or dependence. Policies try to stop addiction, help people get medical treatment, and reduce harm.
pages.caption: Road sign banning cannabis at the Canada-US border.

evidence.articleCaption: Road sign banning cannabis at the Canada-US border.

pages.text: Different places have different rules about what a drug is. Heroin is controlled almost everywhere. Other substances like alcohol or codeine are regulated in some places but not in others. International treaties also help set global drug control standards.
pages.caption: Article 44 of the 1961 Single Convention terminated a number of previous drug-control treaties.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Photograph of the Commentary on the Single Convention on narcotic drugs, 1961 (page 456, article 44).jpg

pages.text: In the 1990s, the United States and countries like Colombia fought against drug cartels. Plan Colombia helped fund this fight to destroy coca crops. While coca cultivation decreased, some farmers who used it for traditional chewing became very poor.

title: Medieval Islamic Geography
sourceTitle: Geography and cartography in the medieval Islamic world

pages.text: During the Islamic Golden Age, Muslim scholars studied geography and map-making. They learned from earlier cultures, explorers, and merchants across Afro-Eurasia. Islamic geography included exploration, physical geography, and mathematical cartography, reaching its apex in the twelfth century.
pages.caption: Map of Fars from the Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (Book of postal routes and kingdoms) of al-Istakhri

evidence.fileTitle: File:Khalili Collection Islamic Art mss 0972 fol 6b-7a.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Map of Fars from the Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (Book of postal routes and kingdoms) of al-Istakhri

pages.text: Geography began in the eighth century with Hellenistic influence. Later, Muslim scholars explored the Muslim world, China, Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa. Important scholars included Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Masudi, and Muhammad al-Idrisi.
pages.caption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

evidence.articleCaption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

pages.text: Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad supported this work. Caliph al-Ma'mun commissioned geographers to measure the Earth and create a large world map. Scholars also inherited works from Ptolemy and adapted them.
pages.caption: Astrolabe from 9th century North Africa

evidence.fileTitle: File:Khalili Collection Islamic Art sci 0430 front.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Astrolabe from 9th century North Africa

pages.text: In the twelfth century, Muhammad al-Idrisi created an important atlas known as the Tabula Rogeriana. Funded by Roger II of Sicily, he combined old knowledge with new reports from merchants to map the world.
pages.caption: Al-Ashraf's diagram of the compass and Qibla. From MS Cairo TR 105, copied in Yemen, 1293.

evidence.articleCaption: Al-Ashraf's diagram of the compass and Qibla. From MS Cairo TR 105, copied in Yemen, 1293.

pages.text: Muslim scholars invented and refined several scientific instruments in mathematical geography and cartography. These tools included the astrolabe, quadrant, gnomon, celestial sphere, sundial, and compass. Astrolabes were widely used throughout the Muslim world as an aid to navigation and to help find the Qibla, which is the direction of Mecca.

Medieval Islamic geography and cartography flourished during the Islamic Golden Age between the eighth and sixteenth centuries. Building on earlier traditions, Muslim scholars advanced map-making through extensive travel and trade across Afro-Eurasia. Their work focused on navigation, physical geography, and mathematical cartography, reaching its peak with Muhammad al-Idrisi.

pages.text: Influenced by Hellenistic ideas, Islamic geography started in the eighth century. Between the ninth and twelfth centuries, scholars traveled widely across the Muslim world, China, Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa. Notable figures such as Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Masudi, and Abu Rayhan Biruni contributed significantly to these developments.
pages.caption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

evidence.articleCaption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

pages.text: The Abbasid caliphs of Baghdad heavily patronized these scientific efforts. Caliph al-Ma'mun commissioned an arc measurement to determine degrees of latitude and calculate the Earth's circumference. While his large world map did not survive, cartographers also adopted Ptolemy's works while introducing their own rectangular projections and adjusted coordinates.

pages.text: In 1154, the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced the Tabula Rogeriana atlas. Funded by Roger II of Sicily, al-Idrisi combined classical geographical data with new information gathered by merchants and explorers, mapping the world in seventy rectangular sections based on climate zones.

pages.text: Scholars also created and refined various scientific instruments for geography and cartography. Devices such as astrolabes, quadrants, and compasses became essential. Astrolabes helped with navigation and locating the Qibla, while early compasses using magnetic needles or iron fish were recorded in the thirteenth century.

C1-C2.headline: Cartography in the Islamic Golden Age

pages.text: Islamic geography and cartography developed extensively during the Islamic Golden Age, traditionally dated from the eighth to the sixteenth century. Scholars synthesized and advanced the map-making traditions of preceding cultures, drawing upon merchant and explorer accounts across Afro-Eurasia. The discipline comprised three major domains: exploration, physical geography, and mathematical cartography.
pages.caption: Map of Fars from the Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (Book of postal routes and kingdoms) of al-Istakhri

evidence.fileTitle: File:Khalili Collection Islamic Art mss 0972 fol 6b-7a.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Map of Fars from the Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (Book of postal routes and kingdoms) of al-Istakhri

pages.text: Beginning in the eighth century under Hellenistic influence, the field expanded as scholars undertook extensive journeys across the Muslim world, China, Southeast Asia, and Southern Africa. Prominent contributors included Al-Khwarizmi, Abū Zayd al-Balkhī, Al-Masudi, Abu Rayhan Biruni, and Muhammad al-Idrisi, who marked the apex of Islamic geographical studies.
pages.caption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

evidence.articleCaption: Diagram illustrating a method proposed and used by Al-Biruni to estimate the radius and circumference of the Earth in the 11th century.

pages.text: Patronage from Abbasid caliphs, particularly al-Ma'mun, was instrumental. Al-Ma'mun commissioned an arc measurement to refine the Arabic mile and calculate the Earth's circumference, alongside a lost world map based on Marinus of Tyre. Simultaneously, cartographers engaged with Ptolemy's Almagest and Geography, adopting rectangular projections and modifying prime meridians.
pages.caption: Astrolabe from 9th century North Africa

evidence.fileTitle: File:Khalili Collection Islamic Art sci 0430 front.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Astrolabe from 9th century North Africa

pages.text: In 1154, Muhammad al-Idrisi compiled the Tabula Rogeriana under the patronage of Roger II of Sicily. Integrating classical data with contemporary merchant accounts, the atlas described a spherical Earth mapped across seventy rectangular sections, utilizing climate zones as a primary organizational principle.
pages.caption: Al-Ashraf's diagram of the compass and Qibla. From MS Cairo TR 105, copied in Yemen, 1293.

evidence.articleCaption: Al-Ashraf's diagram of the compass and Qibla. From MS Cairo TR 105, copied in Yemen, 1293.

pages.text: Mathematical geography and cartography were further supported by the invention and refinement of scientific instruments. Astrolabes, quadrants, and compasses were developed or adopted. Astrolabes incorporated angular scales and azimuth circles for navigation and Qibla determination, while historical accounts document the transmission and use of early magnetic compasses.
